title: Diagnostic Criteria for Diabetes Mellitus and Prediabetes
text:
Normal Glycemia: Fasting plasma glucose (FPG) < 100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L); 2-hour post 75g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) < 140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/L); HbA1c < 5.7% (39 mmol/mol).
Prediabetes (Impaired Fasting Glucose / Impaired Glucose Tolerance): FPG 100-125 mg/dL (5.6-6.9 mmol/L); 2-hour OGTT 140-199 mg/dL (7.8-11.0 mmol/L); HbA1c 5.7%-6.4% (39-47 mmol/mol).
Diabetes Mellitus: FPG >= 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) after an 8-hour fast; 2-hour OGTT >= 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L); HbA1c >= 6.5% (48 mmol/mol); or random plasma glucose >= 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) in a patient with classic symptoms of hyperglycemia (polyuria, polydipsia, unexplained weight loss) or hyperglycemic crisis. In the absence of unequivocal hyperglycemia, results require confirmation by repeat testing.

title: Standard Glycemic Targets for Non-Pregnant Adults
text:
General Non-Pregnant Adult Targets:
- HbA1c: < 7.0% (53 mmol/mol) for most non-pregnant adults to reduce microvascular complications.
- Preprandial capillary plasma glucose: 80–130 mg/dL (4.4–7.2 mmol/L).
- Peak postprandial capillary plasma glucose (1-2 hours after meal): < 180 mg/dL (10.0 mmol/L).
- Continuous Glucose Monitoring (CGM) metrics: Time in Range (TIR, 70-180 mg/dL) > 70%; Time below range (< 70 mg/dL) < 4%; Time below 54 mg/dL < 1%.
Individualized Targets: More stringent targets (e.g., HbA1c < 6.5%) may be appropriate for short disease duration, long life expectancy, no significant cardiovascular disease, provided it can be achieved without significant hypoglycemia. Less stringent targets (e.g., HbA1c < 8.0%) for patients with history of severe hypoglycemia, limited life expectancy, advanced micro/macrovascular complications, or extensive comorbid conditions.

title: First-line and Combination Pharmacotherapy for Type 2 Diabetes
text:
First-line therapy depends on comorbidities, patient-centered factors, and glycemic needs. Generally includes lifestyle modification and Metformin.
Metformin: Starting dose 500 mg once or twice daily with meals; titrate to maximum effective dose 2000-2550 mg daily. Contraindicated if eGFR < 30 mL/min/1.73m2; monitor vitamin B12 periodically.
Comorbidity-Driven Selection:
- Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease (ASCVD) or high risk: GLP-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) with proven CVD benefit (e.g., Semaglutide, Dulaglutide, Liraglutide) or SGLT2 inhibitor with proven CVD benefit (e.g., Empagliflozin, Dapagliflozin).
- Heart Failure (HF) (reduced or preserved EF): SGLT2 inhibitor (Empagliflozin, Dapagliflozin).
- Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) (eGFR 20-60 mL/min or uACR > 30 mg/g): SGLT2 inhibitor with proven renal outcome; if contraindicated or not tolerated, GLP-1 RA.
- Need for Weight Loss: Tirzepatide (dual GIP/GLP-1 RA) > Semaglutide > Dulaglutide / Liraglutide.
- Cost Consideration: Sulfonylurea (Glimepiride, Glipizide) or Thiazolidinedione (Pioglitazone).

title: Insulin Initiation, Titration, and Basal-Bolus Management
text:
Basal Insulin Initiation in Type 2 Diabetes:
- Consider when HbA1c > 10%, blood glucose >= 300 mg/dL, catabolic features (ketosis, weight loss), or when dual/triple non-insulin therapy fails to reach glycemic target.
- Starting basal insulin: 10 units per day OR 0.1-0.2 units/kg/day of long-acting insulin (Glargine U-100/U-300, Detemir, Degludec).
- Titration: Increase by 2 units every 3 days to achieve fasting blood glucose target (80-130 mg/dL) without hypoglycemia. If fasting hypoglycemia occurs, reduce dose by 10-20%.
Prandial Insulin Addition:
- If basal insulin is adequately titrated (fasting glucose in range) but HbA1c remains above target, or basal dose exceeds 0.5 units/kg/day, add prandial insulin (rapid-acting: Lispro, Aspart, Glulisine) 4 units or 10% of basal dose before the largest meal. Titrate by 1-2 units or 10-15% twice weekly.
Type 1 Diabetes Management:
- Multiple daily injections (MDI) basal-bolus regimen (approx. 50% basal, 50% divided prandial) or continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion (CSII / insulin pump).
- Typical total daily dose: 0.4–1.0 units/kg/day.
- Carbohydrate counting: Insulin-to-carbohydrate ratio (ICR) and correction factor (Insulin Sensitivity Factor, ISF) used for meal boluses and hyperglycemia corrections.

title: Management of Hypoglycemia, DKA, and HHS
text:
Hypoglycemia Definition and Treatment:
- Level 1 (Alert): Blood glucose 54–69 mg/dL (3.0–3.8 mmol/L).
- Level 2 (Clinically Significant): Blood glucose < 54 mg/dL (3.0 mmol/L).
- Level 3 (Severe): Cognitive impairment requiring external assistance.
- Rule of 15 Treatment for Level 1/2: Ingest 15–20g of fast-acting glucose (e.g., 4 oz fruit juice, 3-4 glucose tablets). Recheck capillary glucose in 15 minutes; if still < 70 mg/dL, repeat 15g carbohydrates. Once normalized, eat a meal or snack to prevent recurrence.
- Severe Hypoglycemia (Level 3): Prescribe Glucagon (intranasal Baqsimi 3mg or IM/SC glucagon 1mg) for all patients at risk; instruct family/caregivers on administration.
Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) and Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State (HHS):
- DKA features: Hyperglycemia (> 250 mg/dL), metabolic acidosis (pH < 7.30, serum bicarbonate < 18 mEq/L), elevated serum/urine ketones, positive anion gap (> 10-12). Symptoms: nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, Kussmaul breathing, fruity acetone breath.
- HHS features: Severe hyperglycemia (> 600 mg/dL), high serum osmolality (> 320 mOsm/kg), minimal/absent ketosis, altered sensorium/coma, profound dehydration.
- Immediate ER referral and hospital admission required for IV hydration, regular insulin infusion, potassium repletion, and hemodynamic monitoring.

title: Chronic Complications Screening, Nephropathy, Retinopathy, Neuropathy, Foot Care
text:
Comprehensive Annual Complication Screening:
- Diabetic Kidney Disease (DKD): Measure urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (uACR) and estimated GFR annually. Normal uACR < 30 mg/g; microalbuminuria 30-299 mg/g; macroalbuminuria >= 300 mg/g. Initiate ACE inhibitor (e.g., Lisinopril) or ARB (e.g., Losartan) if uACR >= 30 mg/g and patient has hypertension. SGLT2 inhibitors and nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (Finerenone) reduce CKD progression.
- Diabetic Retinopathy: Annual dilated eye exam by an optometrist or ophthalmologist starting at diagnosis for Type 2 diabetes, or within 5 years of diagnosis for Type 1.
- Diabetic Neuropathy: Annual screening for distal symmetric polyneuropathy using 10g monofilament test, pinprick or temperature sensation, and vibration perception (128-Hz tuning fork).
- Diabetic Foot Care: Comprehensive foot evaluation annually; visual inspection at every routine visit. Check peripheral pulses (dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial), skin integrity, calluses, deformities, loss of protective sensation (LOPS). Educate patient on daily foot self-inspection, well-fitted footwear, never walking barefoot.
- Cardiovascular Risk Management: Target blood pressure < 130/80 mmHg. Moderate-to-high intensity Statin therapy for all diabetes patients aged 40-75 years.

title: Medical Nutrition Therapy (MNT), Physical Activity, and Lifestyle Counseling
text:
Medical Nutrition Therapy (MNT):
- Emphasize non-starchy vegetables, whole grains, lean protein, healthy unsaturated fats (Mediterranean or DASH eating pattern).
- Limit refined carbohydrates, sugar-sweetened beverages, saturated fats, and sodium (< 2300 mg/day).
- Carbohydrate consistency: Monitor carbohydrate intake to improve glycemic control and assist insulin dosing.
- Weight Management: Aim for 5-10% weight loss in overweight/obese patients with Type 2 diabetes to improve glycemic control, lipid profiles, and blood pressure.
Physical Activity Guidelines:
- Moderate-intensity aerobic activity: >= 150 minutes per week (e.g., brisk walking), spread over at least 3 days per week with no more than 2 consecutive days without activity.
- Resistance training: 2–3 sessions per week on non-consecutive days.
- Reduce sedentary time: Interrupt prolonged sitting every 30 minutes with short bouts of standing or light activity.
- Hypoglycemia precaution: In insulin-treated patients, check pre-exercise glucose; carry fast-acting carbohydrates.

title: Clinical Note Documentation Format for Diabetes Encounters
text:
A complete diabetes clinical encounter note consists of four structured SOAP sections:
1. SUBJECTIVE / HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
   - Chief complaint (e.g., routine diabetes follow-up, high blood sugar, medication review).
   - Duration of diabetes, current treatment regimen and patient compliance/adherence.
   - Home blood glucose monitoring: fasting values, postprandial values, recent trends.
   - Frequency, timing, and severity of hypoglycemic episodes; hypoglycemia awareness.
   - Review of systems: polyuria, polydipsia, blurred vision, numbness/tingling in hands/feet, chest pain, shortness of breath, leg swelling, non-healing sores.
   - Diet, exercise routine, alcohol and tobacco use.
2. OBJECTIVE EXAM:
   - Vitals: Blood pressure, heart rate, BMI, weight and weight changes.
   - Physical Exam: Cardiovascular, respiratory, abdominal exam.
   - Detailed Foot Exam: Skin color/temperature, presence of ulcers/calluses, pedal pulses, monofilament sensation test.
3. OBJECTIVE RESULTS:
   - Recent laboratory results: HbA1c (current and comparison to previous), Fasting Blood Glucose.
   - Renal profile: Serum Creatinine, eGFR, Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN), uACR.
   - Lipid panel: Total cholesterol, LDL-C, HDL-C, Triglycerides.
   - Dilated retinal exam report date, dental exam date.
4. ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
   - Assessment: Primary diagnosis with type (e.g., Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus without acute complications, uncontrolled vs controlled), current glycemic control status, comorbidity status (hypertension, hyperlipidemia, obesity, CKD).
   - Plan: Medication adjustments (doses, titration schedules), lab orders (repeat HbA1c in 3 months, annual urine microalbumin), referrals (ophthalmology, podiatry, certified diabetes educator / nutritionist), lifestyle recommendations, follow-up timeframe (e.g., return in 3 months).
